cards.title: FPT recovery of graph incidence matrices under low-rank binary perturbations
cards.formal: For each fixed graph class C among all simple graphs, forests, trees, connected simple graphs, and graphs of arboricity at most d for each fixed d≥1, is (min-rank,C)-Graph Recovery fixed-parameter tractable in the perturbation rank r? Given an n×m binary matrix M and r≥0, decide whether there exists an n×m graph incidence matrix S with its graph in C such that rank_{F₂}(M+S)≤r. The target is a deterministic running time f_C(r)(n+m+nm+1)^{c_C}, for a total computable function f_C and a constant c_C independent of r,n,m. Each class is a separate instance of the same question; d is fixed with the class, not an additional input parameter.
cards.why: Would determine whether the algebraic dimension of incidence errors is a usable algorithmic parameter for recovering graph structure, beyond polynomial algorithms whose exponent grows with that dimension.
cards.status_note: Read the full problem definition, incidence/rank conventions, fixed-arboricity case and concluding FPT question. Exact-title, parameterized-recovery and later-work searches through 12 September 2026 found no resolution or later version settling the question. Searches are not exhaustive.

cards.definitions: F₂={0,1} has addition and multiplication modulo two, so M+S=M−S and the perturbation is L=M+S. rank_{F₂}(L) is the dimension of its column space over F₂, not rank over R. The input explicitly lists all nm bits, the dimensions, and r in binary; r may be capped at min{n,m}. The rows are labeled vertices [n] and the columns are labeled edges [m]. An incidence matrix S of a simple undirected graph has exactly two ones in each column, in distinct rows, and no two columns have the same pair of one-positions. Thus loops and parallel edges are excluded; zero rows represent isolated vertices and remain part of the recovered graph. No row operations, vertex deletion, or change in matrix dimensions is permitted. One may choose which pair of row vertices each column represents, so edge labels impose no geometric order. A forest has no undirected cycle; a tree is connected and acyclic; a connected graph has a path between every two vertices, with the single-vertex graph connected. Arboricity at most d means that the edges can be partitioned into at most d forests. Take n≥1 and m≥0; infeasible column counts have the natural no answer. For each fixed C, the required algorithm is one uniform deterministic Turing program for all M,r, with no error. The cost is worst-case bit time. The exponent and parameter function may depend on C, including the fixed d, but the exponent cannot depend on r. The task asks whether a decomposition exists, without promising that the input was generated by a recoverable graph; producing every possible graph is a different enumeration requirement.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove or refute the FPT assertion for the listed fixed classes, reporting which cases each result covers. A positive result needs an algorithm and computable parameter bound with polynomial exponent independent of r. A negative result must rule out such an algorithm for a specified class, with any complexity assumption stated explicitly. General NP-completeness, an (mn)^{O(r)} bound, or polynomial recovery under a bound on the number of flipped entries does not decide this rank-parameter question.

context_blocks.title: The perturbation can be dense but low rank
context_blocks.text: The matrix is the sum of graph incidences and a binary error matrix. Low rank limits the dimension of the error patterns, even when many entries differ. Bounding the number of erroneous entries is a different model and has different algorithmic behavior in the source.

context_blocks.title: The source gives a parameter-dependent exponent
context_blocks.text: For the listed classes, the paper gives algorithms with running time (mn)^{O(r)}. This is polynomial for each fixed rank, but its exponent grows with the parameter. The question asks whether all rank dependence can instead be placed in a multiplicative computable function.

context_blocks.title: Ordinary hardness leaves the parameter question open
context_blocks.text: The source reports NP-completeness for rank-bounded recovery when r is part of the input. This does not exclude an FPT algorithm: such an algorithm may still have a rapidly growing dependence on r. Its polynomial-time results for Hamming-weight-bounded errors do not answer the rank version either.

context_blocks.title: A representation problem motivated by perturbed matroids
context_blocks.text: The paper connects recovery to representations of binary matroids as low-rank perturbations of graphic incidence matrices. It also interprets the task as structured binary matrix decomposition, where the sparse component must be the incidence matrix of an actual graph rather than an arbitrary sparse matrix.

cards.context:
The matrix is the sum of graph incidences and a binary error matrix. Low rank limits the dimension of the error patterns, even when many entries differ. Bounding the number of erroneous entries is a different model and has different algorithmic behavior in the source.

For the listed classes, the paper gives algorithms with running time (mn)^{O(r)}. This is polynomial for each fixed rank, but its exponent grows with the parameter. The question asks whether all rank dependence can instead be placed in a multiplicative computable function.

The source reports NP-completeness for rank-bounded recovery when r is part of the input. This does not exclude an FPT algorithm: such an algorithm may still have a rapidly growing dependence on r. Its polynomial-time results for Hamming-weight-bounded errors do not answer the rank version either.

The paper connects recovery to representations of binary matroids as low-rank perturbations of graphic incidence matrices. It also interprets the task as structured binary matrix decomposition, where the sparse component must be the incidence matrix of an actual graph rather than an arbitrary sparse matrix.

meta.status_scope: No claim of exhaustive open-status verification
methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. We aim for benchmarks of 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. All three use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The possible 1,000-problem expansion has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The targets are 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. Top 100, Top 500 and the possible Top 1000 use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
